reels.title: The crash that paused

prediction.prompt: Black Thursday, 24 October 1929: share prices plunge soon after trading opens. How far down is the Dow Jones average when trading closes?

frames.say: A crowd outside the New York Stock Exchange in nineteen twenty-nine, after the crash.

frames.text: On Black Thursday, 24 October, prices fell 11 percent soon after trading opened.
frames.say: On Black Thursday, the twenty-fourth of October, prices fell eleven percent soon after trading opened.

frames.text: Leading bankers had Richard Whitney, of the Exchange, bid $205 a share for US Steel, well above the market.
frames.say: Leading bankers had Richard Whitney, of the Exchange, bid two hundred and five dollars a share for U S Steel, well above the market.

frames.text: The slide stopped. The Dow closed down only about 2 percent.

reels.title: A parade, not a family line

prediction.prompt: A famous 1965 picture shows apes marching, step by step, into a man. What did the book it appeared in say about the marchers?

choices.label: Each one was the ancestor of the next
Some were side branches or dead ends
Nothing about who descended from whom

frames.text: An ape rises, step by step, into a man at a telescope: a spoof of a famous picture.
Rudolph Zallinger drew the original for a 1965 book. Its 15 figures march as if each became the next.
frames.say: Rudolph Zallinger drew the original for a nineteen sixty-five book. Its 15 figures march as if each became the next.

frames.text: Yet the book's own text called one marcher a likely side branch, and another a dead end.
The artist never meant a single line, its author said. The picture overpowered the words.
Thomas Henry Huxley's 1863 row of ape and human skeletons became an unintended shorthand for evolution, a historian argues.
frames.say: Thomas Henry Huxley's eighteen sixty-three row of ape and human skeletons became an unintended shorthand for evolution, a historian argues.

frames.text: Critics say the march wrongly makes evolution look like progress.

reels.takeaway: The famous march was never meant as a line of ancestors: its own book called one marcher a likely side branch and another a dead end.

sources.claim: It looks like one direct line of ancestors, but the original text knew that reading would be wrong
sources.quote: Contrary to appearances and some complaints, the original 1965 text of "The Road to Homo Sapiens" reveals an understanding of the fact that a linear presentation of a sequence of primate species, all in the direct line of human ancestors, would not be a correct interpretation.

sources.claim: The text called the fourth figure a likely side branch of the human family tree
sources.quote: For example, the fourth of Zallinger's figures (Oreopithecus) is said to be "a likely side branch on man's family tree".

sources.claim: The text called the seventh figure an evolutionary dead end
sources.quote: Likewise, the seventh figure (Paranthropus) is said to be "an evolutionary dead end".

sources.claim: F. Clark Howell, the anthropologist who wrote the section, commented on how it was read
sources.quote: With regard to the way the illustration has been interpreted, the anthropologist and author of the section, F. Clark Howell, remarked

sources.claim: The artist did not intend a linear sequence, but viewers read it that way
sources.quote: The artist didn't intend to reduce the evolution of man to a linear sequence, but it was read that way by viewers.

sources.claim: Howell said the graphic overwhelmed the text
sources.quote: The graphic overwhelmed the text.

sources.claim: Huxley's 1863 frontispiece compared ape and human skeletons, and the historian Jennifer Tucker argues its left-to-right sequence became a shorthand for evolution
sources.quote: Thomas Henry Huxley added a frontispiece to his 1863 book Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature comparing the skeletons of apes and humans, but historian Jennifer Tucker argues that its left-to-right progressionist sequence unintentionally became "an iconic and instantly recognizable visual shorthand for evolution".

sources.claim: The image is Huxley's frontispiece showing the skeletons of apes and man
sources.quote: Frontispiece to Huxley 'Evidence as to man's place in Nature'. Illustration showing skeleton's of apes and man

sources.claim: The March of Progress has been criticised as wrongly implying that evolution is progressive
sources.quote: It has also been criticized as "unintentionally and wrongly" implying that "evolution is progressive".

prediction.prompt: William Herschel claimed to have seen four extra moons of Uranus in the 1790s. What were they, most likely?

choices.label: Real moons, too faint to see again

frames.text: Uranus and its moons, seen by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2023. Ariel and Umbriel were discovered on 24 October 1851.
frames.say: Uranus and its moons, seen by the James Webb Space Telescope in twenty twenty-three. Ariel and Umbriel were discovered on the twenty-fourth of October, eighteen fifty-one.

frames.text: The British astronomer William Lassell found them both.
Two other moons, Titania and Oberon, had been known since 1787. Their discoverer, William Herschel, claimed four more.
frames.say: Two other moons, Titania and Oberon, had been known since seventeen eighty-seven. Their discoverer, William Herschel, claimed four more.

frames.text: If Herschel had seen extra moons, he should have seen these two. They matched none of his four, which were probably faint stars.
Umbriel, named for a gloomy sprite in a poem by Alexander Pope, is the darkest of Uranus's larger moons.

reels.takeaway: Lassell's two new moons of 1851 showed that William Herschel's four extra moons were probably faint stars.

frames.say: Santa María in Guatemala, erupting in nineteen oh-two. It had never been recorded erupting, and was thought extinct.

frames.text: On the evening of 24 October, an ash column rose amid lightning. A ship's captain later put its height by sextant at 27 to 29 kilometres.
frames.say: On the evening of the twenty-fourth of October, an ash column rose amid lightning. A ship's captain later put its height by sextant at twenty-seven to twenty-nine kilometres.

frames.text: The main eruption lasted 18 to 20 hours, among the century's largest. Blasts were heard in Costa Rica, about 850 kilometres away.
It left a new crater, about a kilometre long, seen here full of steam.

reels.title: Leaves that follow the mother

prediction.prompt: Carl Correns found a plant whose leaf colour comes from its mother, not its father. How did he find out?

choices.label: He crossed each colour both ways, as mother and father
He traced the colour through old seed records
He watched its cells divide under a microscope

frames.text: The German botanist Carl Correns rediscovered Mendel's laws of heredity, publishing in 1900.
frames.say: The German botanist Carl Correns rediscovered Mendel's laws of heredity, publishing in nineteen hundred.

frames.text: Then he took on four o'clock plants with green-and-white leaves, which seemed to defy those laws.
He crossed them both ways. Pollen from a green branch, on a white branch's flower, gave white seedlings.
Pollen from a white branch, on a green branch's flower, gave green ones. Colour followed the mother.
Mendel's traits come from either parent alike. This colour depends on chloroplasts, which here come from the mother alone.
His 1909 paper made it the first conclusive case of inheritance outside the chromosomes.
frames.say: His nineteen oh-nine paper made it the first conclusive case of inheritance outside the chromosomes.

reels.takeaway: Crossing four o'clocks both ways showed Correns that leaf colour can come from the mother alone.

m2.alt: Carl Correns, bearded and in glasses and a white coat, handles a small white paper bag on the tip of a tall, prickly stem outdoors; another bag hangs higher up, and buildings stand behind

m1.alt: Portrait photograph of Carl Correns: a man with round wire glasses and a full beard, in a dark jacket

sources.claim: Correns was a German botanist who discovered the principles of heredity independently of Hugo de Vries
sources.quote: was a German botanist and geneticist notable primarily for his independent discovery of the principles of heredity, which he achieved simultaneously but independently of the botanist Hugo de Vries

sources.claim: He rediscovered and independently verified Mendel's work
sources.quote: He rediscovered and independently verified the work of Mendel in a separate model organism.

sources.claim: He published his first paper on heredity in 1900
sources.quote: Correns published his first paper on 25 January 1900, which cited both Charles Darwin and Mendel, recognising the relevance of genetics to Darwin's ideas.

sources.claim: He experimented with four o'clock plants to investigate apparent exceptions to Mendel's laws in mottled green-and-white leaves
sources.quote: he undertook experiments with the four o'clock plant Mirabilis jalapa to investigate apparent counterexamples to Mendel's laws in the heredity of variegated (green and white mottled) leaf color

sources.claim: Green pollen on a white stigma gave white offspring; white pollen on a green stigma gave green offspring
sources.quote: However, if green pollen fertilized a white stigma, the progeny were white, but if the sexes of the donors were reversed (white pollen on a green stigma), the progeny were green.

sources.claim: Mendelian traits do not depend on which parent passes them on, but leaf colour depended greatly on it
sources.quote: Correns found that, while Mendelian traits behave independently of the sex of the source parent, leaf color depended greatly on which parent had which trait.

sources.claim: Seedlings of a green mother inherit working chloroplasts and so are green
sources.quote: Conversely, if a white father is paired with a green mother with functional chloroplasts, the progeny will only inherit functional chloroplasts, and will thus be green.

sources.claim: In most angiosperms the chloroplasts come only from the mother
sources.quote: since the chloroplasts come exclusively from the mother in most angiosperms

sources.claim: His 1909 paper made variegated leaf colour the first conclusive example of cytoplasmic inheritance
sources.quote: In his 1909 paper, he established variegated leaf color as the first conclusive example of cytoplasmic inheritance.

sources.claim: Cytoplasmic inheritance showed that factors outside the chromosomes shape traits
sources.quote: He also discovered cytoplasmic inheritance, an important extension of Mendel's theories, which demonstrated the existence of extrachromosomal factors on phenotype.

reels.title: The sixty percent mistake

prediction.prompt: Suppose personality traits have a heritability of about 0.6. Which reading of that number is right?

choices.label: 60% of your personality comes from your genes
It is about differences between people, not one person
60 in 100 people inherit their parents' personality

frames.text: Two boys, short and tall, hold corn from a short race and a tall one. Height varies in people and in corn.
Heritability is a statistic about such variation. For personality it has been put as high as 0.6, which is easy to misread as 60 percent of you.
frames.say: Heritability is a statistic about such variation. For personality it has been put as high as zero point six, which is easy to misread as sixty percent of you.

frames.text: That reading is wrong. Heritability measures how much of the variation within a population can be put down to genetic differences.
It does not measure how much of one person's trait comes from their genes.
It holds for one population in one setting. It can shift with no change in genes, if surroundings vary more.

reels.takeaway: Heritability describes the differences within a population. It is not the share of one person's trait that genes caused.

m1.alt: Old photograph of two young men beside a measuring pole numbered 1 to 9: the shorter one holds a short corn plant, the taller one a corn stalk taller than himself
m1.credit: After A. F. Blakeslee, in Thomas Hunt Morgan, A Critique of the Theory of Evolution, 1916

sources.claim: The picture shows a short and a tall boy holding stalks from a short and a tall race of corn
sources.quote: A short and a tall boy each holding a stalk of corn—one stalk of a race of short corn, the other of tall corn.

sources.claim: Heritability estimates how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic variation
sources.quote: Heritability is a statistic used in the fields of breeding and genetics that estimates the degree of variation in a phenotypic trait in a population that is due to genetic variation between individuals in that population.

sources.claim: Heritability causes confusion because its technical meaning differs from the everyday one
sources.quote: It is the source of much confusion because its technical definition is different from its commonly-understood folk definition.

sources.claim: Even if the heritability of personality is about 0.6, it is incorrect to read that as 60% of your personality being inherited
sources.quote: For example, it is incorrect to say that since the heritability of personality traits is about 0.6, that means that 60% of your personality is inherited from your parents and 40% comes from the environment.

sources.claim: Heritability measures the fraction of variation in a trait that can be attributed to genetic variation
sources.quote: Heritability measures the fraction of phenotype variability that can be attributed to genetic variation.

sources.claim: It is not the fraction of one individual's trait that genes caused
sources.quote: This is not the same as saying that this fraction of an individual phenotype is caused by genetics.

sources.claim: Heritability should not be read as a measure of how far a trait is genetically determined in an individual
sources.quote: The heritability of a trait should not be interpreted as a measure of the extent to which said trait is genetically determined in an individual.

sources.claim: Heritability is specific to one population in one environment
sources.quote: Heritability is specific to a particular population in a particular environment.

sources.claim: Heritability can change with no genetic change, for instance when the environment contributes more variation
sources.quote: In addition, heritability can change without any genetic change occurring, such as when the environment starts contributing to more variation.
